prompt: What is Microsoft Security Copilot?
choices: A generative-AI assistant reasoning over your security data via plugins
A SIEM that replaces Microsoft Sentinel in the organization's security stack
A CSPM engine that replaces Microsoft Defender for Cloud
A firewall rule engine for east-west network traffic
correctAnswers: A generative-AI assistant reasoning over your security data via plugins
explanation: Copilot reasons over data that other products hold, which is why plugins are what give it reach and why it replaces nothing. Reading it as a Sentinel replacement is the tempting simplification, whereas it depends on Sentinel: with the plugin disabled it can say nothing about an incident at all.

prompt: What does SCU stand for in the context of Security Copilot?
choices: Security Compute Unit
Sentinel Correlation Unit
Secure Configuration Update
Software Compliance Utility
correctAnswers: Security Compute Unit
explanation: SCU is the Security Compute Unit, the provisioned hourly capacity Copilot usage draws on — which is why cost scales with throughput rather than with the number of analysts. The other three expansions are invented, and the Sentinel one is the most plausible of them because SCU sounds like it should belong to the SIEM, whereas it is a Copilot billing unit and appears nowhere in Sentinel.

prompt: How is Security Copilot capacity billed?
choices: By provisioned Security Compute Units, scaled to manage cost
It is included free of charge with any Microsoft 365 E5 license at all
Per user seat, in the way a traditional software license is
Per security incident that an analyst investigates with it
correctAnswers: By provisioned Security Compute Units, scaled to manage cost
explanation: SCUs are provisioned capacity, so cost is governed by throughput rather than by headcount — which is why adding analysts does not by itself change the bill. Per-seat licensing is the tempting model because most Microsoft security products work that way, whereas here the lever is capacity and it can be scaled up or down.

prompt: Build the sequence that makes Security Copilot usable in a tenant for the first time. Not every action in the pool belongs in the answer.
poolItems: Provision Security Compute Unit capacity in Azure
Set the default environment: geo, subscription or resource group, and data storage location
Assign the owner and contributor roles to the right people
Enable the plugins for the products Copilot must reason over
Create a Sentinel Log Analytics workspace for Copilot to write to
Assign an Azure Policy initiative to the Copilot resource group
Request contributor access from Microsoft support
correctOrder: Provision Security Compute Unit capacity in Azure
Set the default environment: geo, subscription or resource group, and data storage location
Assign the owner and contributor roles to the right people
Enable the plugins for the products Copilot must reason over
explanation: Capacity and the default environment are both required before anyone can use Copilot at all, and the plugins decide what it can see once they can. The three excluded actions are each a different misunderstanding: Copilot does not write to a workspace of its own, Azure Policy governs nothing here, and contributor access is granted in the tenant rather than requested from Microsoft — any Entra user can be made a contributor by an owner.

prompt: Where is Security Copilot capacity provisioned?
choices: In Azure, via Create a resource ▸ Microsoft Security Copilot
Inside the Microsoft Entra admin center, on the PIM blade
Inside the Microsoft Purview compliance portal, under settings
Inside Microsoft Sentinel's Content hub, as a solution
correctAnswers: In Azure, via Create a resource ▸ Microsoft Security Copilot
explanation: Capacity is an Azure resource, which is why provisioning happens in the Azure portal even though the product is used elsewhere. The Content hub is the tempting answer because that is where Sentinel content is installed, whereas SCU capacity is billed infrastructure rather than content.

prompt: What does the Security Copilot owner role control that contributor does not?
choices: Settings, capacity, role assignments, and which plugins are enabled
Running an investigation session against the tenant security data in scope
Reading the incident summaries Copilot produces
Using the promptbooks that other people have saved
correctAnswers: Settings, capacity, role assignments, and which plugins are enabled
explanation: The split is administration versus usage: an owner changes what Copilot is, a contributor uses what it already is. All three distractors are usage tasks a contributor can already do, which is what makes them tempting — none of them is what the owner role adds.

prompt: What can a Security Copilot contributor do?
choices: Use Copilot and run investigation sessions
Change which plugins are enabled tenant-wide
Reassign the owner role to another user
Modify provisioned SCU capacity
correctAnswers: Use Copilot and run investigation sessions
explanation: Contributor is the day-to-day usage role: run sessions, ask questions, use promptbooks. All three distractors are administration — plugins, role assignments and capacity — and each is tempting because a contributor is the person who would want them changed, whereas changing them is deliberately reserved to an owner.

prompt: By default, who in the tenant can be made a Security Copilot contributor?
choices: Any Microsoft Entra user in the tenant directory
Only users holding an active PIM-eligible role
Only tenant Global Administrators, and nobody else
Nobody, since contributor access comes from Microsoft support
correctAnswers: Any Microsoft Entra user in the tenant directory
explanation: Contributor is granted inside the tenant, to any Entra user an owner chooses, which is why the meaningful control on data access is plugins and RBAC rather than who holds contributor. The support-request option is the tempting bureaucratic assumption and would make the role unusable, whereas nothing outside the tenant is involved.

prompt: What decides what data and actions Security Copilot can reach?
choices: The plugins enabled for the environment
The user's browser extensions
The Azure region selected for the tenant
The number of provisioned SCUs
correctAnswers: The plugins enabled for the environment
explanation: Plugins gate what Copilot can see and do (Defender, Sentinel, Entra, Intune, Purview, third-party, or custom); browser extensions, region, and SCU count don't determine data/action reach.

prompt: Which of these is a Microsoft-provided Security Copilot plugin category?
choices: Defender XDR, Sentinel, Entra, Intune, and Purview
Only custom KQL plugins built in-house by the customer
None at all, since Copilot has no plugin system
Only third-party SIEM plugins from other vendors
correctAnswers: Defender XDR, Sentinel, Entra, Intune, and Purview
explanation: The first-party plugins cover the Microsoft security estate, and enabling or disabling them is what decides what Copilot can reason about. The custom-only option is tempting because custom plugins do exist, whereas they extend the Microsoft set rather than replacing it.

prompt: Besides Microsoft plugins, what other plugin types can extend Security Copilot?
choices: Third-party plugins, and custom plugins built via API or KQL
Only the plugins bundled with the Microsoft Sentinel Content hub
Nothing, since Copilot cannot be extended beyond its defaults
Only plugins that Microsoft itself has published and signed
correctAnswers: Third-party plugins, and custom plugins built via API or KQL
explanation: Copilot is extensible in both directions: vendors publish plugins, and you can write your own against an API or a KQL query. The Content hub option is the tempting confusion with Sentinel content, whereas that installs detections and workbooks rather than Copilot plugins.

prompt: What is a promptbook in Security Copilot?
choices: A saved, reusable prompt sequence that runs a multi-step task
An autonomous agent that runs unattended, with no prompting from anyone
A billing report of Security Compute Unit consumption
A Microsoft Sentinel analytics rule template for detections
correctAnswers: A saved, reusable prompt sequence that runs a multi-step task
explanation: A promptbook makes a multi-step investigation repeatable, but a person still starts it each time. The autonomous agent is the closest miss and is precisely the thing that does not need starting — that difference is what the objective tests most often.

prompt: What is a Security Copilot agent?
choices: An autonomous worker that runs a security task end-to-end
A saved prompt sequence that a user runs manually each time
A human analyst assigned to Tier-2 triage in the SOC rota
A Microsoft Sentinel data connector for a new log source
correctAnswers: An autonomous worker that runs a security task end-to-end
explanation: An agent works without step-by-step prompting, which is what makes it different in kind from a promptbook rather than merely larger. The saved prompt sequence is the tempting answer and is a promptbook: it still waits for a person to run it.

prompt: Which example best illustrates a Security Copilot agent rather than a promptbook?
choices: A Phishing Triage agent that closes low-risk reports unattended
An analyst running a saved 'incident investigation' sequence each time
An analyst typing a one-off question into the Copilot prompt bar
A dashboard showing Security Compute Unit consumption over time
correctAnswers: A Phishing Triage agent that closes low-risk reports unattended
explanation: The word to look for is unattended: the agent decides and acts with nobody present. The saved-sequence option is the closest miss and describes a promptbook exactly, whereas an analyst has to be there to run it — which is the whole distinction.

prompt: What is the standalone Security Copilot experience?
choices: A dedicated portal with a free-form prompt bar and promptbooks
Copilot panels embedded inside the Microsoft Defender portal itself
A read-only export of Microsoft Sentinel incidents to a file
A Teams bot with no access to any security data at all
correctAnswers: A dedicated portal with a free-form prompt bar and promptbooks
explanation: Standalone is its own portal, which is where open-ended questions and promptbooks live. The embedded panels are the tempting answer because they are the same Copilot, whereas they appear inside another product and are scoped to what that product is showing.

prompt: What is the embedded Security Copilot experience?
choices: Copilot panels inside Defender, Intune, Entra, or Purview
The dedicated standalone Copilot portal and its prompt bar
A monthly PDF security report mailed to administrators
A command-line tool for querying incidents from a terminal
correctAnswers: Copilot panels inside Defender, Intune, Entra, or Purview
explanation: Embedded means Copilot comes to the analyst rather than the analyst going to Copilot, which is why it suits "summarize this incident" in the portal already open. The standalone portal is the closest miss and is the same product in the other arrangement.

prompt: Four descriptions, four Security Copilot concepts. Assign the one each describes; two entries in the list describe none of them.

targets.label: A Copilot panel inside the Defender portal, answering about what is on screen
A dedicated portal with a free-form prompt bar for open-ended questions
A saved multi-step sequence an analyst starts, producing the same steps every time
A worker that investigates and closes low-risk reports with nobody prompting it

explanation: Two axes are being tested at once: where Copilot appears — embedded in another product or in its own portal — and how much a human drives it, which is what separates a promptbook from an agent. The pair most often confused is the last two, since both automate a multi-step task, whereas only the agent runs without being started. The unused entries are the billing unit and an unrelated Sentinel object.

prompt: An analyst opens the dedicated Security Copilot portal and runs a saved investigation promptbook. Which mode is this?
choices: The standalone experience
The embedded experience
A contributor-restricted mode
A read-only reporting mode
correctAnswers: The standalone experience
explanation: A dedicated portal is standalone by definition, and promptbooks are available there. Embedded is the closest miss and would mean the analyst never left the product they were working in, whereas the last two options are not modes of Copilot at all.

prompt: Copilot appears unable to see certain incident data for a user. What should be checked first?
choices: Whether the plugin is enabled, and whether the user may read that data
Whether the user's individual Security Compute Unit quota has been set to zero
Whether the tenant needs to be moved to a different Azure region
Whether the underlying language model needs to be retrained
correctAnswers: Whether the plugin is enabled, and whether the user may read that data
explanation: Copilot sees exactly what the plugin exposes and what the asking user is permitted to read, so those two together explain almost every blind spot. Retraining the model is the tempting AI-shaped answer and is not something a customer does — the failure is a permissions and configuration question rather than a model one.

prompt: Does Security Copilot bypass a user's existing RBAC permissions to answer a question?
choices: No — answers are bounded by the permissions the user already holds
Yes — Copilot holds an elevated identity that ignores RBAC entirely
Only if an owner turns on a permission-bypass setting for the tenant
Yes, but only when the asking user is a tenant Global Administrator
correctAnswers: No — answers are bounded by the permissions the user already holds
explanation: Copilot is a lens over data the user could already reach, so it never becomes a privilege-escalation path. The bypass-setting option is the most tempting because it sounds like a plausible administrative toggle, whereas no such setting exists — which is exactly why granting Copilot contributor access does not widen anyone's data access.

prompt: Which role would be needed to enable a new third-party plugin for the whole tenant's Security Copilot instance?
choices: The Copilot owner role
The Copilot reader role
The Copilot contributor role
Any authenticated Entra user
correctAnswers: The Copilot owner role
explanation: Plugin management is administration, so it sits with the owner. Contributor is the tempting answer because contributors are the people who would benefit from the plugin, whereas using Copilot and changing what Copilot can reach are deliberately separate privileges.

prompt: Which task falls under 'usage,' appropriate for a contributor, rather than 'administration,' which needs an owner?
choices: Running an investigation session and asking Copilot about a query
Changing the default environment's data storage location for the tenant
Provisioning additional Security Compute Unit capacity in Azure
Reassigning which account holds the Copilot owner role
correctAnswers: Running an investigation session and asking Copilot about a query
explanation: Asking questions is usage; everything that changes capacity, environment or roles is administration. The data-storage-location option is the subtlest of the three because it feels like a preference, whereas it determines where data is processed and is therefore owner territory.

prompt: What kind of natural-language request is Copilot well suited to answer about a piece of KQL?
choices: Explaining what the query does in plain language
Automatically rewriting all Sentinel analytics rules
Granting the querying user new RBAC permissions
Deleting the underlying Log Analytics workspace
correctAnswers: Explaining what the query does in plain language
explanation: Explaining a query in natural language is a core Copilot capability; it doesn't rewrite analytics rules, grant permissions, or delete infrastructure.

prompt: A team wants a consistent, repeatable multi-step phishing-investigation workflow that any analyst can trigger the same way each time. What should they build or use?
choices: A promptbook in Security Copilot
A one-off free-form prompt, retyped each time
An Azure Policy initiative on the subscription
A Key Vault access policy for the analysts
correctAnswers: A promptbook in Security Copilot
explanation: The requirement says triggered the same way each time by any analyst, which is what a saved sequence guarantees and a retyped prompt cannot. Note what it does NOT ask for: nobody said unattended, so an autonomous agent would be more than the requirement needs.

prompt: A team wants low-risk phishing reports triaged and closed automatically with zero analyst prompting. What should they deploy?
choices: An autonomous agent, such as a Phishing Triage agent
A Defender for Cloud workload protection plan on the subscription
A promptbook run manually by an analyst each time
A Microsoft Sentinel automation rule on its own
correctAnswers: An autonomous agent, such as a Phishing Triage agent
explanation: "Zero analyst prompting" rules out the promptbook, which is otherwise the right shape and still needs starting. A Sentinel automation rule is the other tempting answer and can set properties or call a playbook, whereas it cannot read a report and judge whether it is phishing.

prompt: Where can autonomous Security Copilot agents come from?
choices: From Microsoft, or from the Security Store
Only from a custom in-house build, never from Microsoft
Only from third-party marketplaces unrelated to Microsoft
Nowhere — only promptbooks can be added to Copilot
correctAnswers: From Microsoft, or from the Security Store
explanation: Agents are published by Microsoft and available through the Security Store, so adopting one is a procurement decision rather than a build project. The in-house-only option is the tempting assumption for anything described as autonomous, whereas the first agents most tenants run are ones they did not write.

prompt: Complete the statement of what must be true before Copilot can summarize a Sentinel incident for a given analyst.
template: The [[b1]] must be enabled, and the analyst must already [[b2]].

options: have permission to view that incident data
hold the Security Copilot owner role
have exported the incident to a promptbook
blanks.correctValue: have permission to view that incident data

explanation: Both conditions are necessary and neither is sufficient: the plugin decides what Copilot can reach at all, and the analyst's own permissions decide what it will show them. Requiring the owner role is the tempting second answer and confuses administration with access — an owner who cannot read an incident still gets no summary of it.

prompt: Which statement best distinguishes an SCU capacity decision from a role assignment decision in Security Copilot administration?
choices: Capacity controls throughput and cost; roles control who administers it
They are one and the same setting, configured together in a single place
Capacity determines which plugins are visible in the tenant
Role assignments determine how many SCUs are provisioned
correctAnswers: Capacity controls throughput and cost; roles control who administers it
explanation: Capacity is a cost and performance lever, roles are an access decision, and neither influences the other. The claim that roles determine SCU count is the tempting conflation and would make cost a function of headcount, whereas provisioned capacity is set independently of how many people hold a role.

prompt: For each statement about the Security Copilot owner and contributor roles, select Yes if it is true.

statements.text: The owner role is required just to run an investigation session.
The owner role is the only one that can view incident summaries.
The owner role can manage which plugins are enabled for the tenant.
The owner role can manage the provisioned Security Compute Unit capacity.

explanation: Owner is an administration role — plugins, capacity, settings and role assignments — and nothing about it is required to ask Copilot a question. The two false statements make the same mistake in different words, treating owner as a superset of usage rights, whereas a contributor already runs sessions and reads summaries bounded by their own data permissions.

prompt: Which two statements correctly distinguish standalone from embedded Security Copilot? (Choose two.)
choices: Standalone is the dedicated portal with a free-form prompt bar
Embedded surfaces Copilot panels inside Defender or Purview
Embedded requires switching to a completely separate portal to be used
Standalone cannot use promptbooks, only free-form prompts
correctAnswers: Standalone is the dedicated portal with a free-form prompt bar
Embedded surfaces Copilot panels inside Defender or Purview
explanation: The two differ only in where Copilot appears. Both false statements invert one property: embedded exists precisely so that nobody switches portals, whereas promptbooks are a standalone-portal feature rather than something it lacks.

prompt: Which two statements about how Copilot's answers are governed are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: Answers are bounded by the querying user's existing RBAC permissions
Answers depend on which plugins have been enabled for the tenant
Copilot holds an elevated identity that bypasses RBAC when it answers a question
The owner role lets Copilot ignore data permissions for that tenant
correctAnswers: Answers are bounded by the querying user's existing RBAC permissions
Answers depend on which plugins have been enabled for the tenant
explanation: Two gates apply to every answer: what the plugin exposes, and what the asking user may read. Both false statements describe a bypass, and neither exists — which is what makes Copilot safe to grant broadly, since contributor access adds no data access of its own.

prompt: Referring to requirement 7 (analysts must ask, in natural language, to summarize an incident and explain a KQL query, from inside the existing investigation portal), which Security Copilot mode fits?
choices: Embedded Copilot, inside the existing Defender investigation portal
Standalone Copilot, opened in a separate browser tab alongside the portal
A Defender for Cloud workflow automation on the alert
A Microsoft Sentinel automation rule on the incident
correctAnswers: Embedded Copilot, inside the existing Defender investigation portal
explanation: The phrase "from inside the existing investigation portal" decides it: embedded panels appear where the analyst already is. Standalone is the closest miss and would answer the same questions, whereas it requires leaving the portal — which is the one thing the requirement rules out.

prompt: Still referring to requirement 7, which plugins must be enabled for Copilot to reason about the Sentinel incident and its underlying KQL query?
choices: The Sentinel plugin, and the related Defender XDR plugins
None at all, since Copilot reasons independently of the source
Only the Microsoft Purview plugin for the tenant
Only the Microsoft Intune plugin for the tenant
correctAnswers: The Sentinel plugin, and the related Defender XDR plugins
explanation: Copilot reads through plugins, so the plugin for the product holding the data must be on. "No plugins required" is the tempting answer if you picture Copilot as a general-purpose model, whereas without the Sentinel plugin it has no access to the incident and can only talk about KQL in the abstract.

prompt: Still referring to requirement 7, if an analyst with only Security Copilot contributor access, but no Sentinel incident-view permission, asks Copilot to summarize a specific incident, what happens?
choices: Copilot cannot surface it, being bounded by the analyst's permissions
Copilot summarizes it anyway, since Copilot access overrides Sentinel RBAC
Copilot grants the analyst Sentinel Reader automatically to answer
Copilot summarizes it only if the analyst is also a Copilot owner
correctAnswers: Copilot cannot surface it, being bounded by the analyst's permissions
explanation: Copilot access and data access are separate: contributor lets you ask, and your existing RBAC decides what you get back. The owner-role option is the most tempting distractor because it sounds like an escalation path, whereas owner is an administrative role and grants no data permission at all.

prompt: Proposed solution: Enable the embedded Security Copilot experience inside the Microsoft Defender portal, with the Defender XDR and Sentinel plugins turned on. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: Yes
explanation: Embedded Copilot puts the prompt where the analyst already is, and the Defender XDR and Sentinel plugins are what let it reach the incident and its query. Note that both halves are load-bearing: the same embedded panel with those plugins off would answer nothing about the incident, whereas the requirement would still look satisfied on the settings page.

prompt: Proposed solution: Direct analysts to open the standalone Security Copilot portal in a separate browser tab and paste incident details manually for summarization. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: This requires switching tools and manually copy-pasting data, which fails the requirement of working 'from directly inside the existing investigation portal.'

prompt: Proposed solution: Grant every analyst the Security Copilot owner role so they can query incidents and explain KQL from within Defender. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: Owner administers plugins/capacity/roles; querying incidents and explaining KQL only requires contributor plus the right plugins enabled and Copilot embedded in the portal — granting owner is unnecessary over-privileging and doesn't by itself embed Copilot in the portal.

prompt: Order the steps for the first-time setup of Microsoft Security Copilot.
reorderItems: Provision/assign SCU capacity in Azure (Create a resource ▸ Microsoft Security Copilot ▸ capacity)
Open the Security Copilot portal for the first time
Set the default capacity, environment/geo, and data-sharing options
Assign owner and contributor roles under Settings ▸ Role assignments
Enable the required Microsoft plugins (Defender XDR, Sentinel, Entra, Intune, Purview) under Settings ▸ Plugins
explanation: Capacity is provisioned in Azure before the portal has anything to run on, the first launch configures the default environment, and roles and plugins follow. Opening the portal first is the tempting order and produces a first-run wizard with no capacity to attach, whereas provisioning first makes the same wizard complete in one pass.

prompt: Order the steps to run a promptbook-based investigation in standalone Security Copilot.
reorderItems: Open the standalone Security Copilot portal
Select or search for a relevant promptbook (e.g. incident investigation)
Provide the required inputs (e.g. an incident ID)
Run the promptbook and review the generated multi-step summary
Take follow-up action in Sentinel or Defender based on the findings
explanation: Reach the standalone portal, find the promptbook, supply its inputs, run it, then act on the output in the underlying product. The last step is the one worth noticing: Copilot summarizes and explains, whereas it does not change an incident — remediation still happens in Sentinel or Defender.

prompt: Configure this simplified Security Copilot settings screen so a SOC analyst can run investigation sessions and use promptbooks, but cannot change which plugins are enabled tenant-wide.
explanation: Contributor covers running sessions and using promptbooks, and plugin management stays off because that is owner territory. Granting owner would satisfy the first half of the requirement and break the second, which is the trap in this screen: the more privileged role is not the safer answer.
